title: Seat Farthest From Everyone
statement:
A row of seats is described by seats: 1 means taken, 0 means empty. At least one seat is taken and at least one is empty.

You will sit in an empty seat and want the person nearest to you to be as far away as possible. The distance between seats i and j is |i − j|. Return the largest distance to your nearest neighbour that you can get.

examples.why: Sit in seat 2, the middle of the three empty seats. Both neighbours are 2 seats away.
Seat 0 has nobody on its left, so the full distance to seat 3 counts. An end gap is not halved.
The middle gap of four empty seats gives only 2. Sitting at the right end gives 3, even though that gap is shorter.

constraints: At least one 0 and at least one 1
hints: For each empty seat, the distance you care about is to the nearest taken seat on either side. How can you get both in linear time?
Look at runs of empty seats instead. In a run of g empty seats between two people, the best spot is the middle, giving (g + 1) / 2 rounded down.
A run touching either end of the row has a person on one side only, so sitting at the very end gives the full length g.

explain.intuition:
Only the runs of empty seats matter. Inside a run of g empty seats with people on both sides, the best you can do is the middle, which puts you ⌊(g + 1) / 2⌋ from the nearer person. A run at either end of the row has someone on one side only, so you sit at the very end and get all g.

So one pass is enough: remember the index of the last taken seat. The gap before the first person counts in full, every gap between two people counts halved, and the gap after the last person counts in full. Take the largest.
steps: For each taken seat i: if prev = −1, the leading run gives i; otherwise the run between gives ⌊(i − prev) / 2⌋. Update best, then set prev = i.
After the loop, the trailing run gives n − 1 − prev. Update best and return it.
pitfalls: Halving the end runs too. In [0, 0, 0, 1] the answer is 3, not 1.
Picking the longest run first and then computing its distance. A shorter end run can beat a longer middle run, as in the third example.
Off-by-one in the middle: two people at prev and i give ⌊(i − prev) / 2⌋, not ⌊(i − prev − 1) / 2⌋.

solutions.title: Nearest person on each side
solutions.idea: Precompute the distance to the nearest taken seat on the left and on the right for every seat. An empty seat's score is the smaller of the two.

solutions.title: One pass over the gaps
solutions.idea: Track the previous taken seat. End gaps count in full, gaps between two people count half.

followups: People keep arriving and each one takes the best seat by this rule, lowest index on ties. Simulate it efficiently. (Hint: a heap of gaps.)
Return the seat index instead of the distance, choosing the leftmost seat on ties.
